card.hook: Picture a huge stone gateway with nothing behind it but open sea, and hardly a crowd in sight. That's Kuninkaanportti, the King's Gate, often described as the island's main symbol and often quieter than you'd expect.
card.stand_here: Stand about 500 m south-east of the subject, at Kuninkaanportti (the phone icon on the map), and face north-west. You're on the seaward side in front of the gate, at the southern tip of Kustaanmiekka, so the stone gateway sits against the sea. It's a walk from the ferry, so give yourself some time.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the gate against the sea. Try 2x or higher (depends on your phone) to get close to the Latin inscription and coat of arms above the arch. Use 0.5x only if you want lots of sea and sky around the gate.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line the archway up with the vertical lines so the stonework stands straight.
card.best_time: Sunset is the one to aim for. In summer, morning light is said to light up the inscription.
card.selfie_here: Go to the arch and the top of the stairs by the King's Gate, face the sea and keep the gateway behind you. Use the front camera, and try 0.5x if you want the whole gate and the walls stretching out on either side in the shot.
card.ask_someone: For a photo of you, try the Great Courtyard: stand near the Ehrensvärd statue so the pastel barracks step down toward the sea behind you, and ask a passer-by to take it.
card.rules_and_safety: Keep to the marked paths on the ramparts and don't clamber on fragile historic structures for a better angle. Drones are generally restricted on the island. Winter snow isn't cleared on the outer fortifications, so wear sensible shoes in cold months.
card.challenge: Get the whole arch, the coat of arms and the sea in one frame without a single stranger walking through it.
card.good_to_know: Suomenlinna is a sea fortress spread across eight islands, about four kilometres south-east of Helsinki city centre. Building began in 1748 under the Swedish Crown, and it became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1991. Today it's as much a picnic spot as a monument.

card.hook: Here's a church where the builders dug a hole in a hill and called it a day, and the bare granite is the wall. It looks a bit unfinished from outside and a lot like magic once you step in.
card.stand_here: Stand about 80 m south-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north-east. From here you get the rocky hill and the church's surroundings in one go, then it's about a 1-minute walk north-east to the church itself.
card.zoom: Use zoom 0.5x for the whole rocky hill outside, and for the dome and rock walls inside. Zoom 1x gives you a natural view, and 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) is great for close-ups of the copper and the rough granite.
card.make_it_pop: Inside, tap the rock wall, then slide the brightness down a touch so the ring of skylights keeps its detail.
card.best_time: Midday is usually a good pick for inside shots because daylight pours through the skylights. Outside, softer morning or late-afternoon light is kinder to the rock. Early is often quieter, but check opening times first.
card.selfie_here: Head to the upper viewing balcony inside the church: up the small staircase to the left of the reception. Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x if you can, and hold it a little low so the rock walls, seating and copper dome all fit over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask someone to stand on the pavement by the main entrance on Lutherinkatu, facing the building, while you pose in front of the entrance so the rocky church fills the background.
card.rules_and_safety: Photos are fine inside, but skip the flash and keep it discreet, and no photos are allowed during services. Large suitcases and backpacks are restricted. Rules can change, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Stand near the middle inside, point your phone straight up, and try to make the skylights form a perfect circle.
card.good_to_know: Timo and Tuomo Suomalainen designed the church, and it was completed in 1969. They dug the main hall out of the granite and left much of the rock showing, with a copper-lined dome on top. It seats about 750 people and is still a working Lutheran parish church. It also had a record 938,000 visitors in 2019.

selfie_spots.why: The balcony gives a wider view of the rock walls, seating and copper dome in one frame, so a visitor can stand there with the church's interior behind them.

card.hook: Everyone calls it the White Cathedral, but it's actually painted in three very similar light greys. Nobody will notice in your photo, but you'll know.
card.stand_here: Stand on Senate Square about 120 m south of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north. You'll be looking straight up at the green dome and the wide steps.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to fit the whole cathedral and its steps. Go to 0.5x if you move closer and want the dome and steps in one frame. Try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for the dome, the columns and the statues on the roof.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, tap the pale front wall, then slide the brightness a little darker so the light grey walls keep their detail and the sky doesn't wash out.
card.best_time: Daytime is best, when the front is evenly lit and the detail looks clean. Early morning is usually quieter on the square. In the evening, try night mode if the building is lit.
card.selfie_here: Stand beside the bronze statue of Tsar Alexander II in the middle of Senate Square, with the cathedral behind you. Use the front camera at 0.5x if your phone has it, and keep the dome over your shoulder. Check the framing on the spot, since the dome needs a little space above your head.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the east side of the square near the University of Helsinki and shoot diagonally across the cathedral steps while you pose on the steps.
card.rules_and_safety: The main steps up to the cathedral are very steep, so take your time on them. Wheelchair access is at the rear entrance.
card.challenge: Zoom to 5x and try to catch one of the Twelve Apostles on the roofline with nothing but sky behind him. Bonus points if you can guess which one it is.
card.good_to_know: Carl Ludvig Engel designed the cathedral as the high point of his Senate Square layout, and the smaller buildings around the square are his too. Building began in 1830, and the church was inaugurated on 15 February 1852. It began as a tribute to Emperor Nicholas I of Russia and was called St Nicholas's Church until 1917.

card.hook: Wood, water, sky: that's the whole recipe at Löyly, and it's enough. The slatted building sits low against the open Baltic, so even a quick snap looks like you planned it.
card.stand_here: Stand about 35 m north-east of the subject, at Löyly (the phone icon on the map), and face south-west. You'll see the slatted wooden wall with the open Baltic behind it.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the main shot of the wooden wall with the sea behind. Try zoom 0.5x if you want the whole sweep of the building from close up, but keep straight lines away from the edges of the frame so they don't bend. Zoom 2x is good for picking out the pattern of the slats.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, put the horizon on the upper or lower line, then tap the sea or sky and slide a little darker so the sunset colours hold and the wood keeps its texture.
card.best_time: Sunset is the time most people recommend. Take a few frames each time, because people will wander through.
card.selfie_here: Head to the wooden waterfront deck next to the outdoor Aito sauna door, with the sea in front of you and the wooden building behind. Use the front camera, try zoom 0.5x, and tuck the building over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask someone to stand near the shoreline facing the building, then take a few steps back so the whole wooden structure fits, with you by the façade; the right-hand corner gives a cleaner line along the wall.
card.rules_and_safety: The roof and some outdoor areas may have access rules, so check the official site before you go. Be polite with people sitting on the steps and wait for a gap rather than asking anyone to move. If you try the sauna, sit or lie down rather than stand, because the head is in the hottest zone and you may feel dizzy.
card.challenge: Find the spot where the curve of the wooden wall leads straight into the sea, and see if you can get the horizon dead level on the first try.
card.good_to_know: Löyly is a public sauna, restaurant and bar on the Hernesaari shore. It opened in 2016 and was designed by Avanto Architects to blend into the park-like coastline. The roof is shaped like a big outdoor auditorium, and Time magazine put Löyly on its 2018 list of the World's 100 Greatest Places.

card.hook: Most people come to a railway station to leave. Here you'll want to stay, because a granite giant with a tall clock tower and two lamp-holding stone figures is waiting out front. About 200,000 people pass through every day, so you'll be in good company.
card.stand_here: Stand at the phone icon on the map, about 130 m south of the subject, and face north. From here the full granite front, the clock tower and the entrance are all in view.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to get the whole facade and tower in one shot. Then try 2x or 5x (depends on your phone) to pick out the Lantern Bearers statues and the clock tower. Use 0.5x only if you walk right up to the entrance.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, line the tower up with a vertical line and hold your phone level so the building doesn't lean.
card.best_time: Daylight shows off the granite best, and a clear day gives you a clean sky behind the tower. After dark, switch on night mode and tuck your elbows against your body to keep the phone steady.
card.selfie_here: Head to the Kivimies (Lantern Carriers) statues at the main entrance. One guide calls them the easiest place for a selfie, with the facade and clock tower in the background. Use the front camera and tilt it so the tower peeks over your shoulder. The platform yard is a second spot to try.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand across the square from the main entrance while you pose by the statues, so the whole granite facade, clock tower and statues fit in the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: Personal photography is generally allowed inside the station, but don't block pathways and be mindful of other travellers. It's a working station, so check the official site before planning indoor photos.
card.challenge: Snap the tower perfectly upright on a gridline with not a single stranger in the foreground. Yes, it takes patience.
card.good_to_know: Eliel Saarinen designed the station, and it opened in 1919. The Lantern Bearers statues by the main entrance are by Emil Wikström. The BBC named it one of the world's most beautiful railway stations in 2013.

card.hook: Uspenski Cathedral sits on its hillside on Katajanokka and just keeps rising above you as you walk up. It's a big, bulky showoff of a building, so even a simple shot from the foot of the hill looks impressive.
card.stand_here: Stand at the phone icon on the map, about 20 m south-east of Uspenski Cathedral, and face north-west. You're close, so the cathedral will fill most of your screen.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to squeeze the whole building in, and tilt your phone up a little. For the upper parts, step back if there's room and try zoom 2x or more, depending on your phone.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, line up one straight edge of the building with a line, and keep your phone as upright as you can so the walls don't lean.
card.best_time: Soft morning or late-afternoon light usually flatters a big building more than harsh midday sun. Earlier in the day is also likely to be quieter, which helps with the passers-by.
card.selfie_here: Try the cathedral hilltop terrace, up the steps from the harbour. Face out over the harbour and city, so the cathedral should be behind you, and use the front camera at 0.5x with the building over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to shoot from the small hillside opposite the cathedral (Kanavakatu 1, Katajanokka) while you stand with the whole building behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: It's a working place of worship. Going inside costs an admission fee outside services, and it's closed on Mondays, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Get one shot where the cathedral's walls stand dead straight against a gridline, with no strangers walking through the bottom of the frame.
card.good_to_know: The cathedral is the main cathedral of the Orthodox Church of Finland and the largest Orthodox church in Northern Europe. It was designed by Aleksey Gornostayev but built after his death, from 1862 to 1868 under Ivan Varnek, and inaugurated on 25 October 1868. About 700,000 bricks came by barge from the Bomarsund Fortress, which had been demolished in the Crimean War.

card.hook: Picture standing inside a shiny steel wave and looking up through hundreds of pipes. That's the Sibelius Monument, and some people see an organ, others see birch woods or reeds on the shore.
card.stand_here: Stand at the phone icon in Sibelius Park, about 15 m south-west of the Sibelius Monument, and face north-east. Walk closer afterwards for detail shots.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole pipe cluster and some sky into one shot. Switch to 1x for a natural view, then try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) for pipe ends and the portrait.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the steel, then slide it a little darker if the shiny pipes are glaring.
card.best_time: Go early morning or late afternoon, when the park is quieter. Softer, lower light shows off the texture of the steel better than harsh midday sun.
card.selfie_here: Head to the Sibelius face sculpture, a few steps from the main steel pipes, and use your front camera with the monument behind you. Zoom 0.5x helps squeeze more of the pipes in over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to shoot from the front of the monument, facing the pipes, so the whole structure fills the frame behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: In winter, take care on the icy rock around the monument. Check access and any local notices before you go, as the park may have work going on.
card.challenge: Step inside the hollow, point your phone straight up, and decide: organ, birch forest or reeds?
card.good_to_know: The monument honours the Finnish composer Jean Sibelius, who died in 1957. Sculptor Eila Hiltunen called her design Passio Musicae, and it was unveiled on 7 September 1967. The wave-like cluster is made of 569 stainless steel pipes welded together and weighs 24 tonnes.

card.hook: Picture a seagull eyeing your pastry while a ferry slides past and gold domes glow behind the market stalls. That's Kauppatori, and yes, the gulls are bold enough to grab food from your hand.
card.stand_here: Stand about 100 m west of the subject, in Kauppatori (the phone icon on the map), and face east. Walk onto the square, stand across from the stalls facing the harbour side, and you'll see stalls up close, then the harbour and ferries, then the Uspenski Cathedral domes.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the whole square. Then try 2x to 5x (depends on your phone) to squeeze the stalls, harbour and cathedral domes closer together. Save zoom 0.5x for close-ups of a stall or the old railway track in the cobbles.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line things up like a layer cake: stalls on the lower line, water in the middle, cathedral domes at the top.
card.best_time: Go between 8 and 11 a.m. on days the market is open. It's busy and the light is soft. The stalls and outdoor cafés run from spring to autumn, so that's when there's the most going on.
card.selfie_here: For a classic, try the Havis Amanda fountain in the middle of the square: the fountain base next to the sea lions is a named selfie spot. For a bigger view, go up to the Uspenski Cathedral upper terrace, face back across the South Harbour with the front camera, and let the square sit behind your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Stand by the stalls and ask someone to shoot from across the square, so the market, harbour and cathedral dome rise up behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: The Havis Amanda statue isn't for climbing, so keep your feet on the ground. If you want to go inside the cathedral, check the official site first, as it has set opening hours.
card.challenge: Find the strip of old railway track set into the cobblestones and get a close-up of it at zoom 0.5x, with your shoe in the shot for scale.
card.good_to_know: The square was built in the 1800s on what had been the muddy bottom of a bay, where fishermen once sold their catch from boats at the piers. About twenty metres of old railway track is still set into the cobbles. A year-round ferry to Suomenlinna leaves from here, and the Presidential Palace and City Hall are right next door.

card.hook: Helsinki locals call it Espa, and it's basically a long green catwalk where the whole city strolls past a bronze poet. Line up the trees just right and the statue looks like it's waiting for you.
card.stand_here: Stand about 160 m west of the subject, in Esplanadinpuisto (the phone icon on the map), and face east. Then walk to the path opposite the Runeberg monument and face it across the path, with the promenade and its walkers behind the statue.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for the statue framed by trees and flowerbeds. Try 0.5x to catch the whole length of the promenade, or 2x (higher if your phone has it) to pick the statue out and soften the busy background.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines to keep the trees upright, and put the statue slightly off-centre with a strip of flowerbed in front.
card.best_time: Pick a quieter time of day for a clear view of the statue. On Vappu (May Day) and summer concert days the crowds can block the classic shot, so shoot from a slightly different angle or come back later.
card.selfie_here: Walk the whole park to the Havis Amanda fountain, where Esplanadi meets Market Square. It's a well-known Helsinki landmark and a good place to stop for photos. Use the front camera, try 0.5x to fit more in, and keep the fountain over your shoulder.
card.rules_and_safety: An audio guide says non-commercial photography is fine at the Runeberg statue (that's not an official park rule). The area is described as well-lit and safe, but keep your belongings secure. For events or temporary restrictions, check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Take a few frames at different heights, and wait for a clear gap in the crowd to catch one walker passing the statue.
card.good_to_know: Esplanadi runs between Erottaja square and the Market Square, right in downtown Helsinki. The statue shows Johan Ludvig Runeberg, Finland's national poet, and was made by his son, Walter Runeberg. In 1827 Engels Teater, the first theatre building in Helsinki, went up in one corner of the park.

card.hook: Oodi is a library that people visit for the building as much as the books, and honestly, fair enough. It's a big, sweeping shape against the Helsinki sky, and it's hard to take a dull photo of it.
card.stand_here: Stand at the phone icon on the map, right at Oodi Central Library itself. You're close, so step back if there's room and face the building so the whole sweep fits in.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to squeeze the whole building in from close range. Switch to 1x for a natural look, then try 2x to 5x (depends on your phone) for details and the view from the balcony.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the building, then slide the brightness down to darker if the sky is washing out.
card.best_time: Daylight shows off the shape best, and softer morning or late-afternoon light is kinder than harsh midday sun. After dark the lit-up building makes a lovely night mode shot.
card.selfie_here: Try the square outside the main entrance, Kansalaistori, under the wood canopy that curves out over the paving. Use the front camera at 0.5x and tilt it up so the curved wood facade is over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask someone to stand on Kansalaistori near the entrance and shoot at an angle to the facade, while you stand in front of the wood wall, so the full curve and you both fit in.
card.rules_and_safety: Keep photo shoots out of passageways and off the staircases, and don't disturb other visitors or staff. Ask before photographing if people are in the background. Photography isn't allowed in the children's section on the 3rd floor. Check the Oodi website before you go for opening times and any photo restrictions inside.
card.challenge: Take one wide shot with loads of sky, then one close-up of a detail, and see if you can make them look like they're from two different buildings.
card.good_to_know: Oodi opened on 5 December 2018, the day before Finnish Independence Day. ALA Architects won the design competition against 543 other entries. TIME magazine listed it among its World's Greatest Places in 2019.

card.hook: Picture a giant wheel, a warm wooden pool terrace and a ferry sliding past behind them. That's the Helsinki harbour postcard, and you can grab it without paying for anything.
card.stand_here: Stand on Kauppatori, about 350 m west of the subject (that's where the phone icon is), and face east across the water. The SkyWheel and the Allas pool terrace sit on the Katajanokka side, with Uspenski Cathedral nearby.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x so the wheel, the pool and the harbour all fit in one shot. Then try 2x to pull the wheel and terrace closer without walking (higher zooms depend on your phone), or drop to 0.5x if you want the square and the cathedral in too.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on your gridlines, put the wheel on one of the vertical lines, keep the pool terrace along the lower third and leave some harbour water in the front.
card.best_time: Late afternoon into evening usually gives softer light and a livelier sky over the harbour. The wheel may look even better at dusk, but check how the light looks on the day.
card.selfie_here: Try the Allas Sea Pool upper roof terrace (Katajanokanlaituri 2a), which you reach after the pedestrian bridge, since the SkyWheel stands right next to it. Use the front camera at 0.5x with the wheel over your shoulder, and check the screen, because we can't promise exactly where the wheel lands in the frame.
card.ask_someone: On the Allas side, ask someone to stand at the corner of the raised wooden gallery/bar and shoot up at the wheel from below, with cranes behind it.
card.rules_and_safety: Allas is a paid sea-pool and restaurant complex, and we couldn't confirm whether you can reach the terrace without a spa ticket, so check on arrival. Photos in the changing rooms and sauna areas aren't allowed, and on the decks and terrace you shouldn't photograph other people without their consent. Kauppatori is the safest spot for photos, and one reviewer called the changing rooms slippery.
card.challenge: Be patient and wait for a ferry to cross behind the wheel, then tap the button just as it lines up.
card.good_to_know: The SkyWheel rises right beside the wooden pool terrace, with the harbour and ferries moving behind it. Together they make one of the city's best-known waterfront scenes. Kauppatori gives you a wider view than the close-up terrace, so your photo says 'Helsinki' and not just 'Ferris wheel'.

card.hook: Red brick, a buzz of market stalls and the harbour right behind: this is the Helsinki photo you'll actually want to keep. The hall looks every bit its age, and the brick glows in a phone photo.
card.stand_here: Stand in Kauppatori (the phone icon on the map), about 120 m north of the subject, and face south. You'll be across the square from the hall's stalls and front, and it's about 2 minutes on foot to the hall.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to get the whole brick front in. Then try zoom 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) to squeeze the hall, harbour and Uspenski Cathedral together. If you're up close and the facade won't fit, drop to zoom 0.5x.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the brick wall, then slide it a touch darker if the sky is bright, so the red keeps its colour.
card.best_time: Go in the afternoon, when the harbour side of the building is in lower light. A travel guide suggests it, and it's kind to the brick.
card.selfie_here: Try the quayside along the South Harbour, next to Kauppatori, so the hall is behind you. Use the front camera, hold it a little low and wide (zoom 0.5x if your phone has it), and let the brick building sit over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand in Kauppatori, across the open square from the stalls, while you pose in front of the stalls with the harbour and Uspenski Cathedral beyond.
card.rules_and_safety: The square and the outside of the hall are open public space. If you want to go inside the hall, check the official site first.
card.challenge: Zoom in a little and see if you can catch Uspenski Cathedral rising behind the hall's busy front, with your gridlines keeping the roof edge dead straight.
card.good_to_know: This is the oldest market hall in Helsinki. Gustaf Nyström designed it in red brick with a cast iron structure, and it opened in 1889, when Finland was a Grand Duchy. It was last renovated between 2012 and 2014, and the hall closed for a year and a half.

card.hook: Picture one of the busiest corners of Helsinki, then a calm, simple wooden building sitting right in the middle of it. That contrast is the fun part, so use it.
card.stand_here: Head for Narinkka Square in Kamppi. The phone icon on the map is at the chapel itself, so there's no walk once you arrive. Step back to the edge of the square and face the chapel to fit the whole building in.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the building and its busy setting. If the square is crowded and you can't step back far enough, try zoom 0.5x, but keep your phone level so the edges don't stretch. Then go to zoom 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) for the walls and the entrance.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line the walls up with them so the building doesn't look tilted, then tap the chapel and make the picture a touch darker if the sky is bright.
card.best_time: Go early in the day or on a quieter weekday if you want fewer people in your shot. Soft, low light shows off the building's surfaces nicely, and late afternoon sun can light the curved walls from the side.
card.selfie_here: Stand on Narinkka Square next to the modern metal sculpture, so the chapel's orange wooden wall fills the background. Or try the steps down from the little piazza on the Simonkatu side, with the chapel behind you. Use the front camera at zoom 0.5x and keep the chapel over your shoulder. These spots are approximate, so wander a bit until it looks right.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand at the northwest corner of Narinkka Square while you pose by the chapel, but check the spot on your map first.
card.rules_and_safety: Photos for personal use are allowed inside, but flash is not. Keep your phone silent, be discreet and respect other visitors. Opening times aren't given here, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Catch the calm chapel and the busy city in the same frame, with one person walking past for scale.
card.good_to_know: The chapel was built as part of the World Design Capital programme in 2012. It was designed by Kimmo Lintula, Niko Sirola and Mikko Summanen of K2S Architects. It was popular straight away, with about 250,000 visitors by January 2013 and its 500,000th a year later. Everyone is welcome, whatever their religion or background.

card.hook: Katajanokka started out as a headland, then a little canal cut across its base turned it into an island. Now you get water, bridges and a whole district rising behind them, often with something working on the water.
card.stand_here: Stand about 580 m west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face east. Walk a little closer along the shore if you want the buildings bigger in the frame.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for a natural view of the water and buildings. Go to 0.5x to fit a whole ferry or the full sweep of the harbour, or try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the cathedral domes or a ship's funnel.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and keep the horizon level, because straight quay edges and bridges look odd when they tilt.
card.best_time: Take a few frames as boats move through and keep the one with the cleanest gap between objects. If you're there at dusk, try night mode and rest your arms on a railing or wall.
card.selfie_here: Try the bridge over the Katajanokka canal, the one that links Katajanokka with Pohjoisesplanadi. Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x if your phone has it, and check on screen that the water is behind you before you tap. I can't promise which way works best, so test a couple of angles.
card.ask_someone: Hand your phone to someone on Pohjoisesplanadi, the street facing the canal, and ask them to shoot toward the canal with you in front of it.
card.rules_and_safety: The waterfront is public space, but ferry terminals and buildings such as the cathedral may have their own access rules, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Catch a boat sliding through the scene with a clean gap on both sides, with water in the foreground and a bridge or ferry as your main shape.
card.good_to_know: A small canal dug in the 19th century makes Katajanokka technically an island, and four bridges link it to the Market Square and Aleksanterinkatu side. The south side is a busy passenger harbour with ferries to Stockholm, Mariehamn, Tallinn and Rostock. The Uspenski Cathedral (architect Alexey Gornostaev, 1868) is one of the district's best-known landmarks, and the older western part is known for early 20th century Art Nouveau buildings.

card.hook: Look up before you walk into the Ateneum. Four stone figures are holding up the pediment, and a goddess of art is blessing the whole show from the very top.
card.stand_here: Stand at the phone icon on the map, about 95 m north-east of the subject, and face south-west towards the Ateneum on the south side of Rautatientori square. From here you can fit the whole building in.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to get the whole facade in. If you're close and the top gets cut off, drop to 0.5x and keep your phone level so the building doesn't lean. Then try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for the busts, caryatids and pediment sculptures.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line the building's vertical edges up with them so the walls stay straight.
card.best_time: Soft morning or late-afternoon light shows off the carved detail. An even, cloudy day works nicely too.
card.selfie_here: Try the pavement of Kaivokatu (the museum's street) with the stately facade behind you. Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x if your phone has it, and hold the phone a little low so the building rises over your shoulder. If you're heading inside, the big staircase in the main hall near the huge windows is a popular selfie spot too.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the opposite side of Kaivokatu from the museum, while you pose in front of the facade.
card.rules_and_safety: Inside the museum, photos are fine for private use, but no flash or selfie sticks. Ask permission before photographing other visitors or staff.
card.challenge: Can you spot all three busts above the main entrance (Bramante, Raphael and Phidias) and get a close-up of each?
card.good_to_know: The Ateneum was designed by Theodor Höijer and finished in 1887. It holds the largest collection of classical art in Finland. A Van Gogh painting arrived in 1903, which made it the first museum in the world to have one.

card.hook: Picture a bronze Mannerheim on his horse, with a very modern, very angular art museum standing right beside him. People argued about that closeness in the 1990s, but it's great for your photos, because old and new fit in one frame.
card.stand_here: Stand right at Kiasma on Mannerheimintie, where the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Keep your back to the south and face the building.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x, because you're very close and you want the whole front in. Then try 1x for a more natural look, and 2x-5x (depending on your phone) for details higher up the walls.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the building, then drag the slider down a touch to make the picture darker if the sky is bright, so the walls keep their detail.
card.best_time: A bright but overcast day gives soft, even light that suits the building well. Go early if you want clear shots without people walking through.
card.selfie_here: Try the main entrance steps on the Mannerheiminaukio side: stand on the stairs in front of the canopy with the building behind you, and use the front camera. The canopy and staircase make a dramatic backdrop, and morning or late afternoon gives the softest light. For a different look, pose on Kansalaistori square against the glass front, which reflects the sky.
card.ask_someone: Ask someone to stand on the north side of Kansalaistori square so Kiasma sits on the right of the frame, with you in the foreground.
card.rules_and_safety: You can photograph the outside from the street. Inside is a public museum, so check the official site for entry and photography rules.
card.challenge: Can you get Mannerheim's statue and Kiasma in the same frame while keeping the building's vertical edges dead straight? Gridlines will help.
card.good_to_know: Kiasma was designed by the American architect Steven Holl. His entry, called Chiasma, was picked from 516 submissions in a competition decided in 1993. The museum opened in May 1998, closed for repairs in September 2014 and reopened in March 2015.

selfie_research.notes: No page I found mentions selfie-stick or tripod rules, so none are listed. Photography policy: a Kiasma FAQ says personal photography is allowed and commercial photography needs permission (https://helsinkicitytips.com/kiasma-museum/); this is not a stick/tripod rule, so it is not in 'rules'. The ask-someone spot is inferred from a Wikipedia photo caption describing the view from the north of Kansalaistori, not from a written instruction. The selfie spots come from listicles and a wedding-photo blog, and none gives exact positions. The rooftop terrace is a viewpoint from the building, not a backdrop with Kiasma behind you, so I left it out.

card.hook: Fourteen tall red granite columns stand in a perfectly straight line, and not one of them is out of step. Parliament House is a photographer's dream because it's so tidy.
card.stand_here: Stand at the phone icon on the map, about 85 m north-east of the subject, and face south-west. You'll see the whole front of Parliament House with the lawn spread out in front of it.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the whole front. If the building won't fit, tap 0.5x to get the full width in. Then try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for the column tops and the statues.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and keep your phone level and upright, because tilting it up makes the columns lean inwards.
card.best_time: A bright, cloudy day gives soft, even light that shows off the red of the granite. Go early if you want a quieter lawn and statues. A guide also suggests the blue hour after sunset for framing the whole building.
card.selfie_here: Try the steps and path in front of the main entrance with the columns and façade behind you. Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x if your phone has it, and let the columns fill the background over your shoulder. You can also stand beside the Mannerheim statue on the square in front of the building.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the street side of Mannerheimintie, where the whole building fits in the frame, while you stand in front of the entrance.
card.rules_and_safety: You can see the outside and the lawn from the public area, but going in needs a tour or visit, so check the official site first. Photos are allowed in some areas inside but not others, so follow the staff or the signs.
card.challenge: Get all fourteen columns in one shot with a president statue in the corner, then count them to check.
card.good_to_know: The building went up between 1926 and 1931 and officially opened on 7 March 1931. Architect Johan Sigfrid Sirén gave it a simple style that mixes Neoclassicism with early twentieth-century modernism, and the red granite comes from Kalvola. The two president statues on the lawn, Kaarlo Juho Ståhlberg and Pehr Evind Svinhufvud, were carved by Wäinö Aaltonen.

selfie_research.notes: No page I found states a selfie stick or tripod rule, so none is listed. The sources are mostly generic travel listings, and the selfie-spot evidence is thin. The Mannerheim statue spot is inferred from a photo caption, not a description of visitor photos. I left out claims I could not support with a named place, including a rooftop terrace (an Access Travel claim that I could not verify and that seems doubtful for a parliament building) and the Oodi balcony view. The supplied coordinates (60.17250, 24.93333) fall close to the building's position given on Wikimedia Commons (60.172253, 24.935191), so they appear to refer to the same site. The geomerid page notes the square in front is used for demonstrations and events, which may affect how busy it is on a given day; this is not a safety statement, so I did not use it as one.

card.hook: Most people hurry across Rautatientori with one eye on the train times. Slow down for a moment: a bronze writer is standing guard in front of one of the best-looking buildings in central Helsinki.
card.stand_here: Stand about 300 m south-west of the subject, in Rautatientori (the phone icon on the map), and face north-east. Then walk to the north side of the square, in front of the main entrance, and shoot from there with the Aleksis Kivi statue in front of you.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to get the statue and the facade together. If the building won't fit, tap 0.5x. For a close-up of the granite or the entrance, try 2x or more.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on your gridlines and line up the building's vertical edges with them, so the facade doesn't lean.
card.best_time: Daytime is the easiest, because the facade is evenly lit. In the evening, switch on night mode and rest your phone against something solid to keep it steady.
card.selfie_here: Beside the bronze Aleksis Kivi statue on Rautatientori, with the theatre's facade behind you. Use the front camera, try 0.5x if your phone has it, and keep the building over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask someone to stand on Rautatientori a little back from the Kivi statue, facing the theatre, so the whole building fits, while you pose beside the statue.
card.rules_and_safety: The square and the statue are open public outdoor space. For performances or going inside the theatre, check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Can you get the statue low in the frame and the facade's edges lined up with the gridlines, with nobody walking through the shot?
card.good_to_know: Onni Tarjanne designed the granite facade in the National Romantic style, and it was finished in 1902. That was the year the company, founded in 1872 as a touring group, finally got a permanent home. It's the oldest professional theatre in Finland that performs in Finnish, and Wäinö Aaltonen's Aleksis Kivi memorial in front of it went up in 1939.
